opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that machine learning isn't just another workload you throw at a general-purpose processor. It has a very particular structure, and if you take that structure seriously, it tells you a lot about what the hardware ought to look like.

When you look at a machine learning model, whether it's a convolutional network, a transformer, or a recommendation model, what you really have is a dataflow graph. Data moves through a series of operators, and those operators are built out of a fairly small set of parallel patterns: maps, reductions, zips, groupBys, and so on. These are data-parallel, highly regular computations, and the access patterns are largely known ahead of time. That's very different from the kind of irregular, control-heavy code that CPUs were designed and optimized for over decades.

So the traditional approach of fetching instructions one at a time, decoding them, and moving data back and forth to a big memory hierarchy wastes a lot of energy and bandwidth on things that aren't actually computation. Even GPUs, which are much better suited to ML, are still fundamentally instruction-driven and kernel-oriented. You launch a kernel, write the results out to high-bandwidth memory, launch the next kernel, read them back in. That round trip to off-chip memory becomes the bottleneck, especially as models get bigger.

What we've argued for a long time, going back to our work at Stanford on Plasticine and the Spatial language, and then at SambaNova, is that the hardware should look like the computation. If the model is a dataflow graph, then build a reconfigurable dataflow architecture: an array of compute units and memory units connected by a flexible on-chip network, where you can map the graph spatially onto the chip and have data stream from one operator to the next without going back out to off-chip memory. You fuse operators together naturally, you pipeline across layers, and you get much better utilization and far less data movement, which is where most of the energy goes.

The other piece is that this only works if the software stack is designed together with the hardware. You need a compiler that can take a high-level description in PyTorch or whatever framework, recognize those parallel patterns, and figure out how to lay them out in space and time on the chip. That co-design between programming abstractions and architecture is really the heart of it.

And there's one more point that matters a lot today: memory capacity. As models have grown to hundreds of billions of parameters, and especially as people want to serve many models or large mixtures of experts, you need a memory hierarchy that holds a lot of parameters close to the compute. So the ML structure shapes not just the compute fabric but also how you think about the memory system.

The big picture is that we're at the end of Moore's Law and Dennard scaling, so you can't rely on general-purpose processors getting faster for free. The way you get performance and efficiency now is by specializing, and machine learning gives us a computational structure that's both very important and very amenable to specialization. Exploiting that structure is the biggest opportunity in computer architecture right now.

r001.rationale: The response says a machine learning model is a dataflow graph whose operators process data in sequence.

r002.rationale: It explicitly advocates building reconfigurable dataflow hardware that mirrors the model’s graph and maps its operators spatially onto the chip.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that machine learning is really a very specific kind of computation, and if you look closely at its structure, it almost tells you what the hardware should look like.

Start with what these models actually do. At their core they're dense linear algebra, lots of matrix multiplies and convolutions, interleaved with relatively simple nonlinear operations. The arithmetic intensity is high, the data access patterns are regular and predictable, and the parallelism is enormous. That's a very different profile from the general-purpose workloads that CPUs were designed around, where you have branchy control flow and irregular memory access and you're spending most of your transistors on caches and speculation just to find a little bit of parallelism. For ML, you don't need to find the parallelism. It's sitting right there in the dataflow graph.

So the first implication is that you should spend your silicon on arithmetic and on moving data efficiently, not on control. GPUs got part of the way there, which is why they've been so successful, but they still carry a lot of the baggage of an instruction-fetch, execute model. If you look at where the energy goes in a modern chip, it's dominated by data movement, not by the multiply-adds themselves. Moving a value from DRAM costs orders of magnitude more than doing a floating point operation on it. So the hardware question becomes: how do you keep data close to where it's being consumed, and how do you avoid shuffling it back and forth through a memory hierarchy that was never designed for this?

That's where I think the dataflow perspective is so powerful. If you take the computation graph of a neural network and map it spatially onto a chip, so that the output of one operator flows directly into the next without going back to memory, you eliminate a huge fraction of that movement. Instead of time-multiplexing a few compute units across a sequence of kernels, you lay the pipeline out in space and stream data through it. The hardware becomes a reflection of the program's structure rather than a generic engine the program has to be squeezed into.

The second implication is about precision and specialization. Machine learning is remarkably tolerant of approximation. You can run inference in eight-bit integers, you can train in reduced-precision floating point, and the models still converge. That's a gift to the hardware designer, because a low-precision multiplier is a tiny fraction of the area and energy of a 64-bit one. Exploiting that is one of the biggest levers we have.

But I'd add a caution, which is that the field is moving fast, and the worst thing you can do is build hardware that's perfectly tuned to the model of two years ago. Transformers didn't exist when a lot of the first wave of accelerators were being designed. So the right level of specialization is not "this chip does ResNet," it's "this chip does the fundamental patterns that all of these models share": the dense linear algebra, the streaming dataflow, the hierarchical parallelism, with enough reconfigurability that you can remap when the models change. That's the balance I think about constantly, specializing enough to get the ten or hundred-x efficiency gains, but keeping the architecture programmable so you don't get stranded.

And finally, I'd say the hardware and the software have to be co-designed. The compiler has to understand the parallel patterns in the model, things like map, reduce, and the hierarchy of nested loops, and the hardware has to expose the right abstractions for that compiler to target. If you design the two separately, you end up with a chip that's impressive on paper and impossible to use. The computational structure of ML is what connects them, so you really have to start there.

r001.rationale: It describes the computation graph of a neural network as the structure used to map its computation onto a chip.

r002.rationale: It advocates mapping that graph spatially onto the chip and says the hardware should reflect the program’s structure.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the computation, rather than with a particular processor architecture. In machine learning, you often have large amounts of parallelism, and you’re applying similar operations to a lot of data. So you want hardware that can exploit that parallelism efficiently.

But arithmetic is only part of the story. You also have to look at how data moves between operations. If you’re constantly moving intermediate results back and forth to memory, that can dominate the cost of the computation. An architecture that keeps data close to where it’s used and passes results directly from one operation to the next can be much more efficient.

The challenge is doing that without becoming too specialized. You want to exploit the structure of machine learning, but you also want enough programmability to accommodate changes in the algorithms. So, to me, the hardware and the software that maps computations onto it really have to be designed together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses operations and how results move between them, but does not identify a dataflow graph as a representation of an algorithm’s computation.

r002.rationale: It advocates hardware that exploits machine learning’s computational structure, including keeping data near its use and passing results directly between operations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the computation itself. In machine learning, a lot of the work involves applying the same operations to large amounts of data. That gives you tremendous parallelism, but exploiting that parallelism is only part of the problem. You also have to get the data to the compute units efficiently.

So the organization of memory and communication becomes central to the hardware design. If you’re constantly moving data back and forth to external memory, you can spend more time and energy moving the data than doing the arithmetic. You want an architecture that keeps data close to where it’s being used, reuses it, and passes intermediate results directly to the next computation when possible.

The challenge is doing that while retaining flexibility. Machine learning models keep changing, so you don’t want to build something that’s excellent at one particular network and can’t adapt. That’s why I’m interested in reconfigurable architectures: you can organize the computation and the data movement to match the structure of the model, with a compiler handling that mapping.

r001.rationale: The response discusses computation, data movement, and intermediate results, but it does not identify a dataflow graph as a representation of the algorithm.

r002.rationale: It says reconfigurable architectures can organize computation and data movement to match the model’s structure, communicating that hardware should reflect the algorithm’s structure.
